case.title: Two places at once: the car park alibi
case.brief: Motor claim. A third party says the policyholder's black SUV reversed into her car at 20:36 on Thursday 17 September 2026, four miles from his flat, and has a photo of the number plate. The policyholder says his car never left its bay in his building's underground car park that evening, and the building has supplied its CCTV. The insurer's position: 'CCTV clocks drift, so this footage could be from any time', and it intends to record a fault claim against him. Establish independently when this footage was really recorded, and whether the car was in its bay at 20:36. Times are UK local time (BST = UTC+1).

input.bottom_line: Car was in its bay at 20:36
input.headline: The flicker of the car park lights shows this footage was recorded on the evening of 17 September 2026, from 20:30:51 to 20:36:51 BST. The SUV sits in its bay the whole time, including 20:36, though the clip stops 51 seconds after that.
input.difference: CCTV clock 2 min 9 s fast; same day, same evening
findings: The car park is underground and lit only by mains-powered ceiling lights. Their flicker carries the grid's frequency pattern clearly and is usable for the whole clip. The clip has no sound.

Matching that pattern against the national grid's second-by-second record (NESO) gives one clear fit: real start 20:30:51 BST (19:30:51 UTC) on 17 Sep 2026, match score 0.98. The next-best time that evening scored 0.65.

Cross-checks: the best match on any other day from 14 to 20 Sep scored only 0.80. The first and second halves of the clip each give the same start time to within 1 second, which argues against splicing. The match falls away sharply a few seconds off the true time.
The on-screen clock runs 2 min 9 s fast, which is ordinary CCTV drift. The real recording time is therefore 20:30:51 to 20:36:51 BST, not 20:33 to 20:39.
20:36:00 BST falls about 309 seconds into the real recording. In every frame I viewed, the black SUV is parked in its bay and nothing about it changes.
input.what_it_means: The insurer's point that 'this footage could be from any time' doesn't hold here. The grid pattern ties the footage to the evening in question to within about a second, whatever the CCTV clock says. The clock was out by about two minutes, and correcting for that moves the clip earlier, not to another day. At 20:36 BST the policyholder's SUV is in its bay four miles from the reported collision. One limit: the real recording ends at 20:36:51 BST. If the third party's 20:36 is a rough estimate and the collision was a minute or more later, this clip alone doesn't cover it. Also, this shows when the footage was recorded and that this car was in this bay. It doesn't show whose car the third party photographed. Plate cloning or a misread plate would need checking separately.
next_steps: Ask the building for a longer CAM 3 export, for example 20:00 to 21:15 BST, plus any camera covering the car park entrance or ramp. That would show whether the car left at any point around the collision, allowing for the 2 min 9 s clock error. I can date-check those exports the same way.
Get the exact time of the collision from the third party, for example from her photo's metadata or a phone call log.
Compare the third party's plate photo with the policyholder's vehicle (make, model, any damage) to check for a cloned or misread plate.
Don't record a fault claim on the assumption that the CCTV time can't be trusted. Its timing has been independently confirmed.
